title: What if we used AI to make everything historically accurate
author: Bintzer
selftext:
This is an underappreciated part of using AI for game dev I feel like. Ive been using it to find and add every piece of historical writing I could find for the area and time period my game is set in. Letters, short stories, poems etc.

It used to be a lot of work to make a game historically accurate down to every detail. A lot of times you’d need specific experts who don’t tend to work at game studios. I see this as super positive, how much more accessible it is now to even try to make a game that’s completely historically accurate. You still have to check what it finds, but you can get pretty far into some really specific stuff now.

I stuffed all those letters and poems onto rocks and into different areas you can explore in the game. They’re part of the worldbuilding now. I also added stuff to the map based on the landmarks mentioned in them. Like there’s a letter from the 1790s about a real mill in Scarsdale, so I put it on the riverbank next to said mill.

My kids like Sleepy Hollow and I live in Westchester near the real Sleepy Hollow. I’ve been learning so much about this area that I never knew before just from making the game.

Highly recommend the approach. I really want to see this more.

comments.author: K_kkomi
comments.body:
This is one of the more interesting uses of AI in game development I've seen. I especially like how you're turning historical documents into things players can actually discover while exploring the world, rather than just using them as background research.

I think this could make exploration feel much more meaningful. One thing I'd be careful about is verifying the original sources, since AI can sometimes mix up dates or present inaccurate information with confidence.

Still, using AI to make this kind of research accessible to solo developers is really exciting!

comments.author: skunk_of_thunder
comments.body:
I can chime in on this.  
I'm working on a simulator for farming in the late 19th century. The core mechanics of the game are already off the beaten path of Godot, so that's been trouble on it's own. The history piece... I made my own wiki just to organize the data. My hope was to have a page for how a piece of the game works, lets say how you actually grew and harvested wheat, with my own textbook citations rather than just Wikipedia's broken link referencing a dead website rewritten from a forum post. It takes a MASSIVE amount of review. It is very quickly overwhelming how much data gets gathered and how much is put in that's just plain wrong. It also read terribly, even after using humanizer tools and many, many passes on the grammar and organization.

I took historically accurate maps of Boston and made... the entirety of Boston, 1890, in 3D. You can get on a horse and ride around. It's cool... but that is also overwhelming. What do you do with it? My original idea was to not have a UI map since it's 1890, GPS isn't a thing, but man... it is way too easy to get lost, and there's nothing to do. It's real world scale Boston, and there's both too much and not enough data on the topic. You are doomed to get both "This is too much content" and "This content doesn't accurately depict history as it was."

Don't mind the fat horse...
